title: Sugar restriction in the first 1000 days after conception, and long-term respiratory health: a quasi-experiment study.
ehr_evidence: Dates of death and causes were obtained by linking to the National Health Service (NHS) death registers in England and Wales, as well as the NHS central registry in Scotland.
summary: Quasi-experimental study linking UK Biobank participants born during UK sugar rationing (1951–1956) to NHS health records to assess the long-term impact of early-life sugar restriction on adult respiratory disease risk, disease onset, and lung function.
key_findings: Early-life sugar rationing (in utero plus 1–2 years) was associated with a lower risk of asthma (HR: 0.75; 95% CI: 0.61, 0.91).
Sugar rationing was associated with a lower risk of COPD (HR: 0.73; 95% CI: 0.62, 0.88).
Rationed participants experienced a delayed disease onset of up to 3.6 years.
Rationing was associated with improved lung function: FEV1% increased by 6.0 (95% CI: 2.9, 9.1), FVC% by 5.9 (95% CI: 3.3, 8.5), and FEV1/FVC ratio by 0.045 (95% CI: 0.011, 0.079).
No significant association was found for idiopathic pulmonary fibrosis (HR: 0.72; 95% CI: 0.46, 1.13; P for trend = 0.145).
Diabetes and hypertension mediated 18.2% of the effect on lung disease risk, while birth weight contributed only 1.6%.
Placebo outcomes (influenza and herpes zoster) showed no significant associations (HRs close to 1).
population: 58,670 UK Biobank participants born October 1951–March 1956, predominantly White, aged 40–70 at recruitment
exposure_domain: early-life sugar restriction/rationing during the first 1000 days after conception
limitations: Unmeasured confounding and secular trends cannot be fully excluded
Right censoring and survivor bias due to lack of prestudy mortality data
UK Biobank is not nationally representative and is predominantly White
Lack of detailed individual-level dietary data
Recall error for early-life variables like breastfeeding status
Use of London air pollution data as a nationwide proxy may not be accurate
Median-based polygenic risk score grouping may not reflect true genetic risk distribution
data_availability_statement: The data are accessible through a public, open-access repository . Data from the UKB, ELSA, and HRS are available to researchers on request.
